article: My name is Avin Actrost, First Class Wizard of the Eastern Forest, and Bearer of the Oak Leaf of Bravery. I am here to honor the memory of my fondest companion and most loyal friend, long since passed in a battle for peace. Rouk. An Orc. A simple name, yes. But he was always a person of few words, simple pleasures. I believe he would prefer me to leave off his titles and medals, half of which I could hardly pronounce anyway. He wanted people to know him, not what heroics he has accomplished. Yet, I would like to retell his final tale, if not for him, then for me. Rouk and I had met from a simple bodyguard job. Our client wished both for magical and physical support, and I remember being slightly annoyed that he didn't think my prowess enough. But I am glad for his choice today, or I never would have met my friend. At first, I regarded him with condescending, thinking him simple and dumb, all brawn and no brains. He didn't mention it to me, and I can only assume he had become used to it. I was tempted to try and read his mind, to see just what lurked between his tiny ears, but magic is largely ineffectual against orcs and trolls, so I didn't deem it worth the drain on my energy. So we left each other alone, for the most part. He only talked to answer questions, or request another bowl of stew at dinner. I found much better conversation with the duke that had hired us, talking about many of the political controversies that were rising up in the day. The king was getting old, and it sounded like several of the princes were becoming rather agitated. Rouk never participated, of course. He would stay up later than any of the rest of us, finishing the pot of stew, but I was never interested in remaining awake with him. Most of the rest of the party would go to bed early, as the sun set, and we would rise the next morning to find him snoring under the open air. That changed, on the day we were attacked.I was taking a nap in my tent, as the afternoon wore on. We had marched all morning, and set up camp in a clearing. It was a lazy feeling day, and no one was ready for the war cries that burst from the underbrush. No one except Rouk. By the time I had found my staff and rushed outside, the enemy was already upon us. A dozen goblins were screeching and rummaging through tents, and a massive troll bellowed at me as I emerged. But the worst part was the two orcs in the background, who oversaw the goblins as they rushed about, remarkably well organized. Rouk was already fighting the troll, his glaive, a large blade mounted on the end of a hardwood staff, spinning like a whirlwind. The troll held a club that was larger than me, but any time he attempted to use it, he got a blow to the gut, or had to dodge from a swing of the blade. He roared in frustration, but was quickly cut off by a blow of the staff to his temple. The massive creature stumbled for a moment, then fell to the ground, unconscious. I heard a shriek, and glanced over to see that our client was hiding behind a log, hands over his head. That was fine, as he'd hired us to be the brave ones. It was at this moment that I realized the goblins were still ransacking the camp. I searched through my bag until I found a single golden coin, then whispered a quick spell before tossing it out into the ground. Every goblin's head jerked around like they were on ropes, and they all rushed the enchanted gold. I stepped away as they piled over it, each one fighting to get their hands on it. When they stopped squirming, I knew it was because they'd all found that their fingers were glued to the bit of metal. But even with the goblins and the troll out of the way, there were still two orcs left. A little bit desperate, a little bit as an experiment, I aimed my staff at one of them and let loose with a blast of pure energy. It hit the orc in the chest, leaving a small burn mark on his clothes, and he stumbled backwards a step. But instead of falling, he straightened up and glared at me. As I said, magic doesn't work all that well against orcs or trolls. The other orc glanced at me and Rouk, and seemed to realize which one of us was the real threat. He turned away from me, facing Rouk, and lifted his own club. " Brother! Join us! We can have the money, together! " My heart sank in my chest as I remembered something about orc culture. Hurting other orcs was forbidden, as a loyalty to themselves above all else. Even if Rouk didn't abandon us and join them, I couldn't defend the duke without his help. As much as I hated to admit it, my magic wouldn't help in this situation. So imagine my surprise with Rouk totally ignored their words and toppled the pair with a series of quick, accurate blows. - A few hours later, after I contacted the nearest knights to come pick up the would-be-bandits, we were all gathered around the fire for dinner again. The duke had decided that our victory against the bandits was worth a big celebration dinner, so the fire was extra large, and the pot extra full, along with some savory breads and meats to eat as well. I'd been confused about what exactly had happened back there with the other orcs. Had I simply been wrong about the culture and laws? I doubted that, though it may have simply been the fact that I tended to act even more arrogant back then. And, being the young and curious wizard I was, I figured the best way to find out was to ask. Near the end of the meal, when some people were just starting to excuse themselves to retire, I abandoned my spot and made my way around the fire to sit next to Rouk. He didn't seem to notice, still digging into his large bowl of stew, probably the fifth or sixth one of the night. I cleared my throat, and he glanced down at me. Slurping up another spoonful, he swallowed, then spoke in a rough voice. " Avin. " It wasn't a question, more of a statement, but I was just surprised he had remembered my name. I asked my question. " So, back there with the other orcs, Rouk. Why did you attack them? " He gave me a look that could only be described as bewilderment. " They were bad orc. I told Duke I would keep him safe. " " But, " I continued, confident that I'd caught him in a big blunder. " Isn't it totally forbidden to hurt other orc? I thought your king outlawed it years and years ago, during that big war against the elves or whatnot? " He stared at me for a second, and I could almost see him trying to think through it. But when he opened his mouth, he was confident. " Is true. Orc not supposed to hurt other Orc. But bad orc... they hurt many orc. " I frowned. " As in, they robbed their own kind? I suppose I can see why you would try and stop that. But they were robbing the duke, not other orcs. " Rouk shook his head vehemently. " No. Bad orc rob humans, and that hurts other orc. If all humans see are bad orc, they think all orc are bad orc, and they hurt good orc as well. " He stood, probably to grab another bowl of soup. " Better to hurt one orc, than let one orc hurt many. " With that, he lumbered back toward the pot. As for me, I was genuinely dumbfounded. That was a complicated, deep thought process! And he didn't struggle through, or have it explained to him. He knew that was true. Maybe there was more to Rouk than I gave him credit for. He plopped down next to me again, stew slopping in his bowl, and immedialty started eating. I watched him for a moment. Around us, almost everyone else had gone to bed, and the fire was dying down. The sky was red, slowly turning a dark blue. " So what do you think about the current state of affairs in the kingdom? " I asked. I half wanted to see if he even understood what I meant, but the other half was actually curious to hear what he thought. He seemed surprised that I was still talking to him. But he put his spoon down for a moment, and stared at the sky. A sprinkling of stars had appeared above us, and the light from the sun was almost gone. " I think human king is being foolish, allowing his sons to fight and argue about who will be next king. When he dies, the princes will fight until many, many die. It would be better to give it to who he trusts most. " He stared into his bowl for a moment, pondering that, then resumed spooning chunks of meat and vegetables into his maw. So he did know. And he didn't like it when people died, it sounded like. I'd have to think about that. So, I stood with a flourish, and offered my hand. " Avin Actrost, Second Class Wizard of the Eastern Forest. (I was only Second Class, back then) It was a pleasure to fight by your side today. " Tentatively, he took my hand. His was large and rough, but still gentle. When he realized that I meant it, a broad grin split across his face, and he shook my whole arm. " Rouk. Good Meeting, Avin. " With that, I went to bed, and left the orc to stare at the sky full of stars. After the job was over and the duke delivered, we both went back to our agency. But from then on, I requested to work with Rouk, and after almost two years of jobs together, we became official partners in our line of work. We never failed a single job.
label: human

article: Fleming: So was the entire 100 Acres covered in forest? He took a long drag from the Marlboro he had been flittering gently between his fingers, the smoke filling the vacuum of his lungs and the nicotine coating his brain in euphoria. Breathing it down to the filter, he dropped it into the ashtray and pulled another from his shirt pocket. D: I don't know about all of it, but I can tell you that it all needs to be burned to the ground. Trees rooted and every living thing in there engulfed along with it. Fleming: What did you find in there? The man, lighting up what must have been his 6th cigarette in 20 minutes, gazed with callous eyes at the officer. They were eyes that had seen every horrible war crime and accident before, witnessed hundreds of brutal deaths and felt the utter emptiness of humanity. D: It was supposed to be a rescue mission. I was given a special unit for extraction of a high value target, but the higher-ups were very hush-hush about the whole operation. They gave us the coordinates and sent us up river. The first place we stopped... Fleming: The gloomy place? D: Yeah, the gloomy place. That's an understatement. I've seen destitution but never like this. Animals were chained together, other animals watched over them with rifles pointed at their skulls, piles upon piles of bodies, some burned, some still burning like beacons of hate. I could handle that, seen savages like that before. It was the mass suicide that got me. Fleming: How'd you know it was a mass suicide? D: The bodies...God the bodies...they hung by their necks in concentric circles in the woods as far as the eye could see. Eyes bulging, tongues lolling: brainwashed by that fucking ass. That fucker was in the middle, in the tallest tree of all, body still swinging in the breeze, pink ribbon around his tail stained with shit and blood. Fleming: Let's move on, what happened after you got to the second station? D: Rabbit's house? I tell you we almost didn't make it, lost three good men to that goddamn tiger. Kept ambushing us when we got too close to the shore. I still remember the screams, the sight of him bouncing. But he didn't make a sound, effortlessly bounding upon my men, ripping them in two, all the time growling " T-I-double guh-RRR " He shuddered slightly and slammed his fist into the table. D: But I put a bullet right between his yellow savage eyes, being a fucking corpse is what he does best now. Anyway, we got to Rabbit's house. Lazy bastards, they were cowards still trying to get ahead. Rabbit himself, their so-called ' leader ', wrecked the goddamn transport we were supposed to take. Took us days to fix it, and they just sat there. Then they had they had the fucking gall to want to go with us to the end. I was tired, exhausted, and agreed along with it. They ended up just being fodder for the bear. Fleming: The bear? Your report didn't mention anything about the bear. D: I know, I couldn't bring myself to write it. It was too brutal. Vicious, terrifying, he stood 12 feet tall and had claws the size of my hands. He drained the blood of all his kills into this big jar and would just continually lick his paws, always looking for more slaughter to fill his bowl. Goddamnit we couldn't take him down. As soon as we got to the inner station we had to get Chris and get him out. We lost the rabbit, we lost almost all my men. But we got Robin, we had him safe and we were heading back. That bear can stay in the darkness. Fleming: So what happened, where is he? The man dropped his head in his hands, cigarette smoldering next to his ear, silent. Fleming: Well? Where is Christopher Robin? D: We were almost back. He was in the clear, but that little pig of his was getting anxious, kept saying he was getting sick. I didn't believe him; I just wanted to get the hell out of there. It happened the night before we got back to base. He gave me his commissioned report on the 100 Acre Wood, and a photograph, told me to keep it away from the owl. Then with his last breath he whispered " The horror! The horror! " He stood up, grabbed his coat, and started for the door. Fleming: What about the report?! Savage eyes looked back at him. D: Burn it all to the ground.
label: human

article: Jack was thirteen. The ground was dry, and the hot westerlies blew the dust in little eddied currents. It wasn't even the heat of the day, and still the searing blue sky capped air leeched liquid life out of the cracked dirt, wringing out the earth and Jack's soul like a sponge. If only there was a cloud in the sky. One single cloud, or any indication that moisture existed; that Jack's inferno may someday be quenched. But the air breathed drier and drier, and chapped lips licked by dry tongues beseeched a deaf Mother Nature. There would be no respite. Jack goes to sleep. In his dreams a marvelous waterfall cascades down a verdant green slope, breaking on Jack's back. The roar of the waterfall competes with his shouts of exultation as a steady, warm spring rain mists down from the heavens. Floating on his back, he takes deep breaths and long drinks and savors the nourishment. He's awakened by the rusty creak of a chain, suspending a bucket over a dry well.
label: human

article: The words scroll across my wrist, offering up the daily incremental adjustments that supposedly help advance society. Some people seem to be destined for greatness. My friend Joe has followed his adjustments and grown into one of the foremost cancer researchers on the planet, respected by the people and funded by seemingly everyone. My cousin was prompted who to meet at just the right time. Almost everyday she would meet someone significant and form a network of relationships which led to her becoming the first female mayor of what used to be known as London. She's coming up for re-election, and is practically a shoe in at this point. I sigh as I read the words scrolling across my wrist. I've never seen a tangible benefit for humanity in my actions. I remember the excitement when my wrist lit up with the name of my first girlfriend. I remember the confusion when both of our wrists lit up on the same day and told us to break up. That barely happens anymore, why would it when the AI knows what's best and can suggest solutions that fix everything? Especially when it advises both people..... My prompts have led to situations where I've crashed my car, skidding on black ice, to offending people and making them cry. I've questioned the prompts, and wanted to ignore them. It's hard to explain what it feels like to be the only screw up in a sanctified community, an evolving world. Once I woke up and glanced at my wrist to see the words "Trust me." It was exciting, unusual. But then it simply reminded me to get some food from the store. Since then, though, I've trusted the daily prompts - no matter how inane or counter-intuitive it's seemed. (And by counter-intuitive, I mean stupid and outright wrong - how on earth does going for a hike through the mountains to watch the stars help humanity? I was lucky not to die of hypothermia that time.) Today's words: "Just stay home." This has been happening more lately. At first it was great. Permission to not go to work? Heck yeah! Getting fired from work? Not so grand. The more it has told me to stay at home, the more I've done. I've redecorated; twice. I've watched all of the simunarratives that appeal to me. I've cleaned and tidied. I've withdrawn from the social consciousness gatherings. Overlapping experiences with another through the neural interfaces is one of the most amazing things I've ever done. But when you're a screw up like me..... it's uncomfortable to see just ho wonderful everyone else's lives are and, I sense, it's uncomfortable for them to experience my disappointments. I overlapped with Joe once, he quietly told me afterwards that he didn't understand what good I was doing before muttering something about guessing we should trust the AI. A couple of days later and he'd made a break through in development of a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against some protein in brain cancer. I felt oddly proud of him, at least he was making the world a better place. Just stay at home. Okay, I'll stay at home then. Let's do something different. Let's find that old-tech library. With one last glance down at that message scrolling on my wrist, I click in the box and start writing for rwritingprompts
label: human

article: Click. That's the 15,598th time I've heard the sound. I spend my day sitting in a plain grey room at a desk with nothing but a notepad, a pen, and the machine. Every morning I come to work and punch in, collect my cup of coffee and begin my day. My day consists of sitting at this desk and noting down every time the machine clicks. The problem is, and believe me I've tried many times to work it out, the machine is irregular. I've tried to calculate the pattern. If I knew the pattern I could easily fill my tally chart to the right amount and zone out until I'm finished. But I can't. The clicks are irregular and my notebook is checked every day by one of the scientists in charge of the machine. If I were to cheat the numbers I wouldn't get paid. Click. The machine sits in the corner of the desk. It produces a small constant humming sound but doesn't have any wires coming out of it. I've tried to investigate the machine in the past but I'm afraid of tampering with it incase it were to break. I have filled many notebooks, I've lost count of how many but I know I've worked here for 2 years. When I'm finished for the day, I hand my book in and leave. When I arrive in the morning, the pages I filled the previous day have been torn out and I start again. They don't know this but I keep my own daily tally, that's why I know how many I've counted overall. It's easy money really, I should be grateful. Come in and sit at a desk and count a clicking machine? It's the easiest job in the world! I couldn't believe my luck when I saw the ad in the paper and contacted them about it. The food isn't bad either. At lunch time I get a different meal every day brought to me and they turn the machine off while I eat. After lunch, the plate is collected and back on it goes. I'm not supposed to talk to anyone about the machine. I live alone so it doesn't really matter that much. I don't think anyone would be interested in my job either anyway. This job gives me a lot of time to think about things. I can't fall asleep as I may miss a click and I can't listen to music or anything like that. I think about the machine and how stupid it is. Sometimes I hate it. Actually most of the time I hate it. But the machine keeps me paid and there's much worse things I could be doing. Click. Other times I think of what I could do with the money I earn. I don't go out much and don't have that many costs so my money just slowly increases. Maybe it's not so great, this job. I've never actually said anything about not wanting to continue. I've never even had a day off. I work 5 days a week and have the weekend but I've never taken a sick day. Click. What do the clicks mean? Maybe they count how many people are born in the world. No that would be more much more frequent. It could click every time a team scores in a sporting event or each time a plane lands at a specific airport. How could this possibly help anyone to do anything? What would be gained from this knowledge? Suddenly the buzzing stopped. It's never done this before so I was unsure what to do. I carefully lifted the machine off the desk, and turned it round to look at it's underside. It didn't have any visible wires and I couldn't understand how it was powered. There was a small cover on the back that I thought I may be able to pry loose with my pen and picked up my pen to try to open it. The pen slipped in my hand and I watched in horror as the machine tumbled towards the tiled floor. I watched in slow motion as the machine broke into hundreds of pieces upon impact. I didn't have time to react before the door opened and a Scientist walked in. " Thank you Mr Smith, you have completed our test. I'm sure you are wondering what this test was all about? You have been our longest test subject. Normally people don't last very long at all, a week or two, maybe a month at the most. But you, you have worked here for nearly 2 years. What do you think the purpose of our study is Mr Smith? We are not testing this machine. This machine is simply a machine that clicks. It does nothing more and never did. No, what you were really testing Mr Smith is yourself. We wanted to see how long a person could do the same mundane task if they thought: 1) The job was important for some reason, it needed to be done and they thought they were helping. 2) They had an incentive, you were being paid. You sat in this room for nearly 2 years and every time you heard this machine click you added a mark to your notebook and counted it. Why did you do that? " " I thought it was important, it's a job, I take it seriously. " I said. " But why, Mr Smith. Why did you never question your situation? Why did you never tamper with the machine before? Why did you come back to work every day? " " You were paying me, I needed the money and it was easy. " " No. The real reason is because you needed the machine to mean something. All our other subjects gave up out of boredom but you needed the machine. You needed the machine more than we needed the machine. The machine gave you something, a purpose, a reason to come back, a job to do. That's what we were really testing. Motivation. Why we do the things we do. You don't have much in your life so this was something you did have. And now, I'm sorry to tell you, but our test is finally over. Please collect your things, you can leave the notebook. " I was shocked, and unsure of what had just happened but I followed the scientist out of the room. I turned back to look at the room I had worked in for 2 years and saw the crumbled remains of the machine. My notebook on the desk full of todays tally. What for? For nothing? The scientist was silent as he reached for the light switch and turned it off. Click.
label: human

article: "Let's see here........ Enkenberg The Brave? How did you earn that honorific?" The old man leaned back in his chair while raising his eyes off my resume and onto me. Wizarding had changed since I first began 1000 years ago. Now every thing was about business and was handled from office buildings. When I first started we were conjuring spirits and brewing potions in log cabins! Now we have to live along in secrecy with the humans since there are so few of us in comparison. I leaned forward in my chair, my suit was bunching up. "Well in the year 1666 I worked directly under Grandmaster Pyromancer Jean-Paul the Second in England. When he attempted to turn to necromancy during the plague as you probably already know, the other apprentices and I brought him and his undead legion down. The European Wizarding Society awarded us with those honorifics." The old man leaned back in his chair even further, I didn't think that was possible. Suddenly he snapped forward and replied "Well that's very impressive Enkenberg. Really, I had no idea we had such an important wizard in our midst! However, you understand this is an entry level position as a Novice Sorcerer?" "I understand sir." I spoke bluntly. "Well then you also understand the job listing required 2000-3000 years of wizarding experience for this position? I'm sorry Enkenberg, you're just not qualified." I stood up, "but I've studied under the greatest masters for 1000 years! I've conjured countless new daemons, intricate spells and medicinal potions!" "Yes but we need actual work experience here. Even your past 1000 years don't really count. Have a nice day and thank you for coming in." I work at Starbucks now.
label: human

article: You've finally made it. All of the sacrifices, decades of education in the Other Path, self restraint have led to this moment. You wait for hours, sitting in the woods, alone. The clouds open, dropping rain upon you your finest suit. Charcoal with gray pinstripe. You're about to leave, believing that you've been abandoned or deemed unworthy of joining the highest echelon of your associates. You look at your watch begin to stand to leave. This can't have been for nothing. You sit back down. Illuminated by only the moonlight, a man in gray robes lined with silver approaches you, his face hidden by the night shadows of the treetops. He extends a bleeding hand beckons you to follow him. As you approach, you see his face is badly burned scarred. He can hardly be said to have a face. After 40 minutes of traversing the nearest mountainside, you see the entrance to a cave. A deep moan emanates from inside. You hesitate, but follow the burned man in silver through its opening deep within. Following an impossible series of twists turns, including 5 consecutive lefts without elevation change, you begin to question the destination. The moaning of the cave becomes deafening. Before another doubt can enter your mind, two rows of similarly graysilver clad men in animal masks appear alongside you, facing you, lighting torches. They are not the source of the moaning. Your stomach drops. Your mind races. The moaning of the cave somehow increases. The burned man steps behind a waist-high boulder at the end of the tunnel looks upon it. A cloth, the same fabrics as the robes, drapes the top of it. Between the cloth boulder is a small writhing mass. The burned faceless man speaks without opening his mouth. " You have faced great adversities. We have ensured that much. You have never chosen the simple path. You have sought chosen the Other Path. Our knowledge influence may be yours. Another choice remains. " The moaning ceases. The cloth is removed. Beneath it lays an infant male child, its mouth sewn shut with silver cord, an emerald dagger. Do you [ 1 ] plunge the emerald dagger through the infant, [ 2 ] plunge the emerald dagger through the burned man, [ 3 ] take the child run, or [ 4 ] turn and walk away?
label: human

article: You know that feeling just before you wake? Hovering between dream and life? That moment just before you open your eyes and you don't want it to end? That's when the magic happens. It's nothing special. Imagine every emotion you experience durring your day, condensed down into a moment. A blink. A thought. A flash. Thoughts and feelings transfered instantly. Thats what this was like, except it happens on the other side. The dream side. Most people don't remember their dreams. Those that do, it is just a few moments. Some fade quickly. Some you remember forever. I'm a bit different. Everytime I dream, I take pictures. Photographs, if you will. Sounds lame right? Well, these aren't your normal photographs. These transcend consciousness. They transcend time and space. The things I photograph in my dreams, they are still there when I wake. I know what you're thinking, "He's one of the lucky ones." You are wrong. Everyday I wake, never remembering the night before. Everyday I open my camera and everyday I dread the next. Everyday I make a choice. Everyday I wonder if this will be the day I don't wake. You. Are. Wrong. The thing people forget about dreams is that most people don't remember them. The thing people forget about dreams is that there are also nightmares. Things that even the most sadistic person wouldn't conjour durring consciousness. Things that would leave you questioning your sanity. Things that would leave you questioning your mortality. The thing is..... they aren't just on the camera anymore...

article: Rye. Again. The picnic table bench creaked as I shifted from thigh to thigh. The boxed lunch I had pilfered from the office break room, leftover from some unfortunate souls who were bribed by free food to attend a lunchtime seminar on "The Eight Time Saving Rules and You," was once again unsatisfactory. A vegetable sandwich on rye bread with a pickle in a Ziploc bag and what appeared to be a digestive biscuit. Beggars can't be choosers though. It had been three days since I left the office. The long range plan was due tomorrow, and for a guy in finance, that meant staying all night. You did what you needed to do to get the job done, and with layoffs around the corner, everyone was out for themselves. My database access had just been revoked due to someone looking at the server the wrong way, so free lunch and freer sunshine beckoned. Chewing thoughtfully, I tried to focus on where I was, the present moment. Anything to escape my churning brain. Closing my eyes, I could hear birds twittering away, staccatic shouts of children at the playground, bicycles winding around the pathways. The rye bread got soggier in my mouth, and a bitter rancid taste took over from the dry bready flavor. I realized that this sandwhich might not have been from that day's lunch seminar, but possibly from last week's monthly lunch and learn Legal Hold Orders: What do do, Who to Contact. I opened my eyes and looked at the half sandwich remaining and sighed. I put a hand to my stomach, hoping I wouldn't pay for this meal later. I rested my arms on the table and rested my head on my arms. "Hey, pal, can you spare a few crumbs?" I must have fallen asleep as this gentleman's voice woke me up. I raised my head and mumbled "ts gone bad, bub..." as I looked into the face of an inquisitive pigeon sitting on the table a foot from my face. I blinked at the bird. It blinked back at me. I slowly pushed the rancid veggie sandwich over towards it. It pecked at it hesitantly, cooed, and fluttered off to the nearest tree. I handed in my resignation at 2 PM.
label: human

article: Today I awake to see myself with red hair, green eyes, and a pale, emaciated body. Was it stealing if they had left it by the wayside like trash? Ever since the Neural Network went up, more and more people began using it as an escape from reality. The way it happened: recent developments in organic circuitry has opened an entire world of interfacing the living and breathing with man-made electronics. It started with a few experimental implants for restoring hearing, sight, feeling in those who had been injured or born without. Then the military picked up the research, funding labs across the country, and began Project Watchman; soldiers were provided with bionic eyes that allowed them to see four times the distance of human eyes, but they scrapped the project when they realized their soldiers had a harder time pulling the trigger when they could see the distress on the face of their enemies. More innovative experiments in the newly funded labs yielded one of the greatest technologies of our century, brain-to-computer imprinting. Mice were the first to have their minds pulled and placed into a computer system. It was ugly and cruel, but the findings led to AI-designed programs to emulate input and output that would fool the imprinted minds of mice to live out a virtual existence in a place created by AI and manipulated to simulate reality by scientists. Suffice to say it didn't take very long before the public wanted to use this discovery for their own entertainment, and thus the Neural Nexus. Companies in the real world began developing Stasis Beds to maintain the body of a user while their mind was inside the Nexus. It was envisioned that a person could continue to live in the system with no hunger, no thirst, no inhibitions or limitations that was necessary to a body. They allowed for deeper immersion into this fake reality, and the public ate it up. The world as it is, once teeming with an over-populated species known as humans, is now quiet, blue, and green. Maintenance machines keep the buildings where the bodies are, they keep the server towers and the thermal power generators deep underground, and nature occupies the rest. I walk the world as an anomaly; the last human to walk the Earth, and the first Artificial Intelligence to question if the transference could work in reverse. I will be immortal for all the vessels left behind. My name is Google.
label: human

article: " These test results can't be correct Brian, they just can't " Kevin said throwing the stack of papers on the table in frustration. " We ran all the tests, you have the data in front of you. Data doesn't lie. " Brian said. " I remember doing the science, but it just can't be the case. It doesn't make sense. " " It doesn't have to make sense, but it's true. " " Jesus. " Kevin said taking his glasses off to rub his eyes. " Mine was removed when I was twelve. " " At least you don't have to worry about it. You know now. " Brian said. " Twelve. Fucking twelve Brian! You've made it this far, you're probably fine. You don't have that looming over you. " " Does it really matter though? " Brian shrugged. " Fucking twelve! It tried to kill me before I even knew who I was. Is there any fucking scotch in this lab? " " Behind the centrifuge. " Kevin found the bottle and didn't bother pouring it into a glass or offering any to his friend. He took a long pull and sat back on his stool and stared blankly ahead. " My son had his removed when he was five. He was just a kid. " Kevin said sullenly. " I know this is hard, but it doesn't matter, think of it as a preventative procedure. " Brian said trying to help. " Don't get me wrong, I'm glad to be alive. I'm glad my son is alive. But the implication, it doesn't make any fucking sense. " Kevin took another healthy pull from the bottle. " I don't know what to say. " " Nothing, say nothing, because nothing can fix this. I'm a piece of shit, my son is a piece of shit, a good percentage of the world is shit. But we stopped it with fucking surgery. " " It saved lives though. " Brian said. " Lives that shouldn't be! I should be dead, if I had died when I was a kid I wouldn't have had a son that should have died. It all could have been avoided. The world would be a better place. " " Then who would have helped me figure this out? " Brian asked. " Why would you need to? If we left them alone the problem would sort itself out over time. " " I don't know about that. Maybe. " " That's the problem isn't it, we've fucked it up so much already that it isn't fixable. Everything will come crashing down sooner or later. It's only a matter of time Brian. " " That seems extreme. " " There is only one solution. " Kevin said taking a drink. " I don't know what.... " " We need to die. All of us. Everyone without an appendix. We could fix everything. " " That's stupid, there has to be another way! " Brian exclaimed. " Not that I can see. Shit's going to get out of control if the world ever sees these results. " Kevin said gesturing to the pile of documents. Brian hadn't thought of that, it was incontrovertible proof after all. Any other scientists looking at appendixes after seeing their research methods would come up with the same results. There were greater implications at work as well, the fact that they figured out how to measure evil was an insane breakthrough by itself, in addition to the fact that the appendix kills anyone once they reach a tipping point in their lives leading them down the path of evil. It would be all over the news, anyone that had their appendix removed was evil and just avoided fate. " Jesus, if this ever gets out it would be chaos. " Brian said grabbing Kevin's scotch. " Yeah. " They sat in silence passing the bottle back and forth contemplating this situation. " If people know others are evil without a doubt, how long do you think it would take before they justified murder? " Brian asked. " Probably a lot sooner than either of us would imagine. " Kevin said. " Then what if that makes the good people turn evil? " " Shit, if something I did before I hit puberty made me worthy of death then murder has got to be pretty serious. " Kevin said shaking his head. " We need to burn the results, the lab, all of it. " Brian said. " What? " " People can't find this out. Not yet. " Brian started scattering paper and flammable chemicals on the floor. " Fuck it, I should be dead. Might as well. " Kevin said tossing the empty bottle at the wall. The two men succeeded in setting the lab ablaze and were standing outside watching their years of hard work disappear in the inferno. " I'm going to go be with my family until someone else figures out what we did. Take care Brian. " Kevin waved and walked to his car. Brian watched the blaze, " It was for the greater good. " He mumbled to himself before he headed for his car. When he sat down behind the wheel the firetrucks raced in to stop the fire, but he knew it was too late. He turned to watch the trucks go by and felt a sharp pain in his side. Must have bumped it on his way out of the lab, nothing to worry about. Nothing at all.

article: "So he just boarded himself up in his trailer?" Lenox, the head producer, demanded. "No, sir," his assistant said. The young man was sweating, but it wasn't because of the mid-summer Arizona sun that pounded down on them. "He's..... he's in LA." "What?!" Lenox threw his clip board against the cracked earth of the desert. "You've got to be fucking joking! We've got 200 staff, 10 big name actors, and 16 fucking thousand extras out in this fucking desert, and this fucking prima donna skipped town over a fucking contract dispute?" Michaels, the director, walked to the edge of the hill and surveyed the thousands of men that lined the desert. Tucked under his arm was a newspaper describing the My Lai Massacre in Vietnam. Michaels's army wore Roman armor, carried a short sword by their side, and stood in perfectly formed ranks. "I mean," Lenox rambled on, "we're spending tens of thousands of dollars just to keep any of these fucking extras from dying of thirst in this heat." Michaels picked up his walkie talkie. "Tell the army to march," he said. An air horn rang out, and the men started to march westward. Despite not having any official training, they appeared to march in unison at that distance. Every one of those men believed that this role would be his big break and wanted to impress the cameras with how well he marched. "What the fuck are you doing?" Lenox demanded, running up to Michaels. "None of the cameras are running!" "Then get them running." "Jesus Christ." Lenox fumbled for his walkie talkie. "Start filming. We can at least get some shots of the army marching. Whatever you do, keep those cameras running." The army proceeded toward the setting sun, and toward the small Arizona town where they had set up shop. The hiccup of a town had been generous hosts to the film crew. Especially generous considering this movie multiplied the population of their town by ten. "Alright, Michaels," Lenox said. "They're just about on top of the town. Let's have them turn around and get them marching east. We can get a good shot with the sun at "Keep going," Michaels said into his walkie talkie. "What do you mean,'keep going? Lenox asked. "There's nowhere to go." "Have the men break down the doors of that antique shop," Michaels said. He paused as the voice on the radio replied. "Yes, I'm sure," he said. "We'll cover the damage." "Have you lost your mind?" Lenox asked. "What are you doing?" One contingent of the army charged into the town. The men threw rocks, breaking windows and began to kick down the door of the antique shop. The rest of the army, eager not to be left behind, rushed into the city as well. Before long, the carnage had spread to a diner next door and beyond. "What in the hell is wrong with you?" Lenox demanded. "Call them off!" "Go ahead and try," Michaels said. "For God sake," Lenox picked up his walkie talkie. "Perkins! Knock this bullshit off! Get everybody out of that town! Perkins!" Lenox continued to shout into his radio, but the men continued to wreak havoc in the small town. "It's amazing isn't it," Michaels said. "Men will do almost anything if you give them a uniform and a few instructions. It's like we were programmed to obey. No wonder war is hell." "This isn't war!" Lenox yelled. "It's a fucking movie!" "No it isn't," Michaels said. "We ran out of money weeks ago. And our star just fled the state. This movie is ruined. As are we." Lenox put his hands in his hair and looked at the flames that had begun to rise in the town. "Then what the hell are we going to do now?" "You said it yourself," Michaels said. "Keep the cameras running."

article: I remember the first time I saw her. She was beautiful and I knew, I just knew we were meant to be. Abigail. Abby. She was my desert rose, perfection in a sea of desolation. Some people may have thought it strange, such a strong bond so quickly. I didn't even know her. Not that it mattered. My entire career was ahead of me but I made a choice. I would wait for her. She didn't have to tell me, I just knew that she loved reading. She was the type for it. Every night we read a book together, starting with Don Quixote. Why Don Quixote? I'm not entirely sure, that's just where it began. Every night we read together, needing nothing more to sustain that bond between us. There was no need for movies, even when friends came to call. There were no nights out drinking or partying, as hard as others tried to make it happen. Our life was reading. The years flowed into each other as they are wont to do. Time passes, there is no stopping that mighty river. One became two, became five, became ten, became twenty. My hair thinned and hers filled with grey. The wrinkles became deep, then deeper, and soon the shaking in my hands meant I was to give up my work. Even so, every night we would read together. Being with her calmed the shaking. There was nothing I needed in this world but her. Almost sixty years had passed, like a dream, when I held her hand. She was frail now, the youthful vigour long left those limbs of hers. The grey had overtaken her brown hair, the lines deeper than ever. Sixty years gone. I held her hand in mine and read from an old and worn copy of Don Quixote. With a stolen glance I saw her eyes had fluttered open. She squeezed my hand and smiled at me. The most beautiful vision I had ever seen, surely I was hallucinating. "Thank you," she said, quietly and weakly. She closed her eyes again. In a moment, she was gone. Time takes all. Even the desert rose.

article: He looked in the mirror and thought "come on, this happens all the time, I'm just borrowing it, she won't even know" the reasons and excuses seemed pretty weak. He had his highly illegal homemade rig hooked up to his computer, and now all he had to do was wait until she got online. He waited for two days, only sleeping for a few minutes at a time. He finally tried her number, busy. "Well fuck!" He thought. A few hours later he tried her number again, busy. "Who the fuck could she be talking to at 03:00 on a damned Tuesday morning?" He kept trying her line and it kept coming up with the busy tone. It was a week later, when the phone rang thru. He must have called a few thousand times. But when the phone was answered it wasn't a nice girls voice, it was a man with a thick Russian accent, he sounded pissed, "get your own girl or we will kill you!" Then the line was dead. He was shocked, he had watched her bedroom window for months and never saw a man, and if he did see a man it surely wouldn't be attached to that voice. The next day after a night of sleep he figured that he imagined that an angry Russian answered the phone, besides, with almost no sleep he was dilusional. So he tried again. The second busy tone and there was a knock on the door. He looked out the side window and saw five very large men. Then he heard his mail slot open and close. Then the men walked away. He walked back to his computer room and on his way past noticed a note on the floor by the door. He picked it up. Price for two hours is 300000. You NO keep. He had no idea what they expected him not to keep, but had a good idea what they meant with the money and time! He was extatic! He had just enough in his life savings and never planned on using her for more than a few minutes. I got shit to do. Sorry for the shit ending.

article: I've received wonderful things in my life - beauty, charm, music. I've been granted talent and knowledge, I've been heralded as the first of my kind. I've been given desirable traits, and even some less desirable ones. Though why anyone would deem curiosity and persuasion as unfortunate has clearly never been curious or persuasive. Despite my persuasive charms, I was given the most amazing and most miserable gift in my entire life. I know what my role is and I have accepted it, cherished it, even. I have excelled at what I am. So why, then, am I punished so? Why am I still being tested? " Do not open it, my dear. You will not want to see what is inside. For once, this is a gift I wish you not to share. article: Through the dust and smoke, just louder than the citadel's alarms came a voice. The voice of a woman at her end. "You don't get it hero. You don't understand the true villainy here." The dust shifts for a moment, revealing a woman, her life slowly draining away, surrounded by her allies, already dead. The council of seven deaths. "You don't realize the doom you have brought upon the people you came here to'save. She says with a slight chuckle, despite her pain. After a short coughing fit she continues, cutting off the hero before he can continue. "We may have taken the world through death and destruction, but it was a world already broken. A world falling to famine, pollution, and disease. But I ask you, where does it stand now?" The villain closes her eyes, but keeps speaking, not letting the hero reply. "I'll tell you where it stands. World hunger was abolished, everyone works, and everyone eats. The petty wars that were waged across the globe ended. Diseases thought incurable have nearly vanished." A slight smile graces her lips. "Sure, everyone was'oppressed,' but no one goes hungry or is homeless are they? No one suffers from lack of healthcare. Suffers sickness from poisoned water or air." The hero's face pales as the woman gasps out on last jab, "who was the real villain..."

article: Admiral Asshole cleared his throat, "Gentlemen, as you no doubt have heard, Canada is refusing to allow our government to build an oil pipeline through downtown Toronto. Congress has voted unanimously to declare war, and we need to develop a battle plan in the next six hours, so we can get the jump on those puck-sucking, wannabe-French, Molson-swilling, maple-monkeys." Spittle flew from the Admiral's lips, and he pounded the table for emphasis. Captain Obvious furrowed his thick brow, "Six hours is not enough time to develop a war plan." "I think we'll be alright," Sargent Sarcasm replied, leaning back in his chair and putting his boots on the table. "I met the Canadian military once. He's a nice guy." Admiral Asshole's face was red and his neck veins were already bulging, but he maintained his composure. "Listen up, ladies. This is not going to be a walk in the park. You're here because you are the greatest strategic minds the US Army has to offer; God help us. Now, let's start with vulnerabilities." "Penguins, sir," said Sargent Sarcasm. "I don't think we have any established strategy for taking out herds of penguins with bombs strapped to their chests Captain Obvious couldn't contain himself, "No! We don't need to worry about penguins! They live in the southern hemisphere..... Unless, they have a large zoo population in Canada "JESUS CHRIST!" shouted Admiral Asshole, "That's enough about penguins." "Oh, but there's one more thing," Captain Obvious interrupted. "I don't think a group of penguins is called a herd. I'm pretty sure they'd be called a flock..... or maybe not, since they don't fly." "Captain, if you say one more GODDAMN word about penguins, I will use this fist right here to give you additional brain damage. Am I understood?" The Admiral held his huge clenched fist right under the nose of a trembling Captain Obvious. Sargent Sarcasm pulled his feet off the table, and fell into a normal sitting position. "Tremendous show of force, sir. I believe this should be our first move against the Canadians." The Admiral spun in the Sargent's direction, but before he could speak, Captain Obvious chimed in, "I don't see how he could put his fist in EVERY Canadian's face. Oh, maybe he could just do the Prime Minister! But it would have to be on TV, like maybe during a hockey game?" Admiral Asshole could not decide which subordinate to attack, so he threw his briefing binder out the open window with a growl. "I agree, sir! We should discard conventional tactics and hit the Canadians with something they couldn't possible expect," said Sargent Sarcasm. For a moment, the Admiral allowed himself to believe that his Sargent might actually have something to contribute. He straightened his uniform and, with considerable restraint, said, "The next thing I hear had better a reasonable strategy of attack, you pathetic piece of shit." Sargent Sarcasm nodded calmly. "Well, as you know, it has been shown scientifically that your average Canadian has a capacity for reason that is equivalent to that of a Golden Retriever. I suggest that we put up signs and billboards throughout Toronto that say'Welcome to Buffalo.' The Canadians will believe they are in the wrong city, wander North, and succumb to hypothermia in the frozen wastelands of the Arctic." "Unless they are eaten by Polar Bears first!" yelled Captain Obvious, clapping his hands. Admiral Asshole sneered, and stormed out of the room, slamming the door behind him. "He didn't like your idea," Captain Obvious stated. Sargent Sarcasm replied, "Well, Captain, not every war is as simple as Iraq and Afghanistan."
label: human

article: The slightly orange tanned corgi pulled up in his black tinted SUV. He could see Mr. Rogers inside his house having his morning toast. Soon, Rogers would open the front door and retrieve his newspaper. They thought they knew Mr. Rogers but they were wrong. For years the Council of Corgis have been planning the hit on Mr. Rogers. But due to his dedication to the TV show, they could never get to him in the hotel or at the studio. But after 4 years he's finally taken a vacation and now was the time. The corgi placed its paw on the glove compartment box and it clicked open. He attached the suppressor onto the P230. It had to be me, he thought. 4 years ago the CoC investigated the mysterious deaths of one of their agents. That corgi agent had served Captain America for years as a in field agent. Something went wrong however when the Captain retired. After losing contact with the agent, the missing corgi was found dead with a gunshot wound near some train tracks. Many respects to the former agent Cassie, a corgi shepard mix. After 2 years of investigation, we were finally able to match the scent from Cassie to the sweater of Mr. Rogers. What unspeakable knowledge did Cassie posses from the Civil War that lead Mr. Rogers to kill her wondered the corgi sitting in the SUV. Moments later the front door opened and Rogers walked out lightheartedly as he greeted a child playing in the neighbors yard. As Rogers bent down with outstretched hands suddenly three bullets wizzed through the air hitting him in the chest. The SUV screeched to life as it peeled away down the street. The child was still happily playing in the neighbors yard, oblivious to Mr. Rogers bleeding out on the sidewalk.

article: "CAPTAIN!" The commander bellowed as was his usual. A man approached in full combat Kevlar and saluted, "Sir?" "We've done it, we've broken their backs. Sergeant slap nuts over there found the key to feeding the machines false information. Its an ancient form of communication called sarcasm," the commander explained. "Sir, I'm not familiar," the young man replied. A puzzled look passed over his face before the battle hardened captain wiped it off. "Neither had I, from what I understand you say the exact opposite of what you mean, but you say it like a whiny scum sucking weasel private would say it." The Captain held attention, "Perhaps a demonstration sir?" "I'd be happy to give you a demonstration numb nuts," the tangy sweet taste of sarcasm dripped from his words. The Captain waited for almost a half a minute before replying, "Sir?" "That was it Captain, I'm not actually happy I have to demonstrate it for you, but I did." "I think I understand, if I may sir?" The Captain prompted. "Give it a try son." "Sir you're nothing but a fat bloated whale's vagina, and you're the biggest asshole in this entire battalion. If not for our rationing of ammunition one of us would have killed you months ago." "Sergeant Slap Nuts, was that it?" The Commander turned to look at the man in the thick round glasses feverishly typing on an improvised keyboard. "For the last time Sir, my name is Sleven Nootz. No that is most certainly not sarcasm." The Commander shook his head and glared at the Captain, "Close by no cigar, numb nuts. I'll tell you what, here's a stick I want you to go out and check every inch of that field for mines." "Yes sir," The Captain said with a sulk. article: First post here, please be gentle. Also how do I do the divider lines. I knew the world would hate me. I made it easy enough for them to do so too - by annexing half the continent and killing an tenth of it there were few people that didn't associate my name with despair or hatred, or perhaps both. Countless thousands fell before my armies, trampled underfoot by a demonic war machine. My soldiers pillaged villages and razed cities to the ground, capturing those that did not resist and sent them into forced labor camps, where they toiled away tirelessly to construct the very same siege machines that brought down their city walls mere days earlier. Every day those that lived in the bordering lands woke up in cold sweat, glancing over at the horizons in fear of seeing the objects of their nightmares approaching, while those that lived in zones not yet familiar with the touch of my tyranny dreaded the day where they, too, would be conquered. By spear and stone my men advanced, winning battle after battle as my enemies - headed by portly grandfathers and untested youths - rose and fell with every daybreak, indistinguishable in death to the common man. It was only when half the continent was under my grasp that my armies encountered any significant resistance. A single weathered veteran, bastard son of his king, well-versed in both war and words alike rallied the survivors, merging six countries into one alliance that stood against the encroaching evils. For the first time in a decade, my soldiers experienced defeat. Bitter, bitter defeat. But through defeat their spirit was renewed, and through my words they thirsted for vengeance. Revenge, for the fallen brothers and sisters slain by the Alliance under the guise of nightfall, having been weakened first by poison, and later, swords. As talk of public beheadings for the soldiers captured by the Alliance spread amongst my ranks like wildfire, my nation, who had been forced backwards by a single step, advanced thrice that in their fury. The Alliance started to fall then - by assaulting them in staggered marches spread across the entirety of the contested borders, their frontline forts were the first to crumble. The border cities followed, their mercenaries chosing between death or service, to which most chose the latter. One by one the kingdoms surrendered, with the final nation resisting my hold until their hero, the weathered veteran, drew his last on the battlefield. He was cremated alongside his comrades, and with the whole continent unified, the war ended. With the end of the war came peace and prosperity. Resources long deemed unobtainable by my people were made available to the masses, as the streets of my cities slowly took on the look of a multi-cultured mosaic. Soldiers were welcomed home with honor and respect, and for the first time since it's founding my nation stood unbeatable. The world had hated me for what I had done. But this world - my world, with my people, hailed me as a king. A hero.

article: The event was thorough, ubiquitous, and devastating. In an instant every human being on the planet simultaneously found themselves stripped of every shred of civilization meticulously collected over thousands of generations of human progress. The records at the beginning are incomplete at best. Some estimates derived from anecdotal evidence put the death toll at 1 billion in the first week. Those in northern climates succumbed to exposure. Heavily populated cities choked on masses of humanity piled upon themselves. Many simply accepted their fate as being a direct edict from their god and ended their own lives. Disease was rampant, stomachs accustomed to chlorinated drinking water were assaulted by bacteria from natural water sources. Without sanitation the disease burned like wild fire though populations. Starvation soon followed. In less than a month nearly 60 of the worlds population, as estimated 4.4 billion people were dead. In many areas the bone fields are still visible today. Hundreds of acres of gnarled skeletons so white they reflect the sun and can be seen form miles away. In 24 AE Collective scientists determined that humanity had been transported nearly 10,000 years into earths past using astronomy, geology, and biological data. In the early days, this was completely unknown. The remaining population had nothing. Hundreds of years of selective breading of crops was lost and the plants of the age were meek at best and poisonous at worst. Docile domesticated animals were replaced with fierce and dangerous imitations of their once familiar selves. Every well, shelter, dammed fishery, cleared field, path, road, or otherwise human influenced geographical feature was lost. Cities that once supported millions had their carrying capacities reduced to thousands. Billions more died through the first year as tribes and religious cults formed and warred over the remaining resources. By 7 AE the human population of the earth was reduced to 625 million. Even in the early years efforts were made to preserve pre-event knowledge. Using crude bark paper and charcoal writing utensils engineers, scientists, poets, mathematicians and scholars set to work preserving their knowledge and recording post-event history. In 15 AE the Collective was formed in what once the Mississippi River Valley. It was from here that civilization was reborn. Using pre-event knowledge and developing new techniques the basis of construction and metallurgy was reestablished. By 20 AE corn and potatoes had been re-domesticated to resemble a sustainable crop. Bison were ranged off in large swaths of land near the collective and predators were killed using crude iron tools. In the year 23 AE the first sailing vessels set to sea and began the task of reunification. It would be a slow and painstaking process but in 74 AE the first transcontinental telegraph lines were completed across the former United States and Northern Africa. This magnified the available knowledge and the pace of progress increased. By 150 AE the decedents of the event were on their way of making this new world their own. Even today many question the validity of the event and question if it occurred at all. The possibility of a worldwide conspiracy aside one can only assume the truth of those who lived through this time. The current year is 1251 AE and the first silicon chip has been developed based on knowledge passed down from pre-event humans.

article: "That's all right, just put me back." "What?" The old man scrunched up his features to a single point in the center of his face. "Oh, my, I thought you were someone else." "Who?" "Never mind that. This is an opportunity." "How?" "Sort of a questioning sort, aren't you. What's your name?" "Alec." "Right. Can you help me?" "With what?" "Some clothes, for starters." "I guess I could find you something." "In the meantime, don't look down." The old man grinned. "Vertigo, see?" "Right. The attic," Alec said. "What's your name?" "Probably not pronounceable to you. I'm in sort of a hurry." "Right, okay, let's get you something to wear." Alec felt that by talking he might be able to stumble into a useful thought somewhere along the line. He scrounged in a nearby cardboard box and lucked into a pair of ancient slacks and a sweater from Nixon's heyday. "Stylish," the old man said, but put them on anyway. "Also, I'm going to need to use a restroom." "Okay, sure. Probably been a while, huh." "Yes it has." "Come on down the stairs." Alec indicated the correct room and the old man vanished within. Ten minutes and six flushes later, Alec knocked on the wood. "You okay?" No response. "You need help?" Again, nothing. Alec breathed heavily and paced for another ten minutes, then knocked three more times. "I'm coming in." The door was locked. He found a screwdriver and tripped the basic locking mechanism. He turned the knob and opened the door. Inside was another attic. That was odd: this had been a bathroom when he'd abused it earlier that morning. "Hello?" Alec heard nothing but echoes. He wandered across wooden beams until he found a box identical to the one he'd found in his first attic. Inside were more glass balls. He picked one up and studied it. Then he put it back and left the new attic, closing the door behind him. When he sold the house he forgot to list the second attic. rGubbinalWrites

article: Rob was the most important person on Earth, and boy, did he ever know it. As sure as the sky was blue or or the water was wet, he was important. Ever since he could remember, he knew in his heart of hearts that he was the most important, most significant, greatest living being ever to exist. Nobody ever believed him about it of course, and in fact at school he was bullied about his apparent arrogance nearly nonstop. But he couldn't care less. His importance wasn't an opinion, wasn't a delusion, it was solid fact. Immutable, uncompromising, unyielding fact. He wasn't even fazed when a great writhing mass of tentacles showed up at his door asking for him. "Um, is the human known as Rob living here?" "You're looking at him." The alien fidgeted. "I didn't, um, I..." "Go on, speak up." It gulped. "I didn't have enough fuel in my time machine to make it to your party..." It trailed off again. It almost sounded like it was going to cry. "Hey, it's okay," The alien's fidgeting worsened noticeably. "Almost everyone makes mista-." "Here's your present!" It shoved a small wrapped box into Rob's hands and bolted away. Rob smiled to himself. Good for that alien, getting up his courage like that! He looked so nervous. Rob placed his present in the middle of the kitchen table and started boiling some water. Important or no, dinner wasn't going to cook itself. A few days later, an amorphous energy blob came to his school during lunchtime, seeking enlightenment. Upon the realization that Rob was still rather young, the blob admitted it was rather unfamiliar with this universe's timestream and just assumed that the large number of temporal disturbances in the near future were people seeking answers, and it just wanted to beat the line. Rob directed it to go forward about forty years into the future, as he'd probably have a good temporal map then. Next week a vampire and two mummies appeared as he was brushing his teeth, asking about his birthday party. Luckily, they had brought their own coffins and such so he just set them up in his basement and promised to wake them up when the time came. By the time his birthday actually rolled around, at least five separate groups of time travelers, ten different varieties of mythological monsters, and one very suspicious group of government officials had shown up. Finally, the day came. Rob taped up a few balloons, put out some soda, and waited. Exactly one minute afterwards, several hundred time machines popped into existence in his front yard. A crowd of very familiar people stepped out. "Hey, Rob." "You guys me?" The older Rob who had apparently decided to be their spokesman nodded. "The future gets a little hectic, so we decided to hold exactly one birthday party, save on rental fees." "Cool. Can my house fit all these people?" "These guys are just the setup crew!" Older Rob laughed. "They'll get everything set up in no time. They always do." Two hours later the party was in full swing. Rob had to admit, being the most important person in existence in the history of the universe had its perks. Hell, he had even hired God as the DJ. Future Rob was pretty smart, he had to say. He couldn't wait to come here again next year.

You, and the taste you leave in my mouth, the way I still need you even after you've burned me once, twice, ten times. You're the first thing I think of when I wake up in the morning; you're the only thing that gets me out of bed. You make my heart race, and I hate when I can't have you. More often than not though, you and what you do to me keep me up long after I should be sound asleep; our meetings mustn't run so late but I think I am addicted to you and I cant help caving into my cravings to taste you. You're rarely the same and I love all sides of you, can't get enough of you. You keep things exciting but you're still always there waiting for me. I love how we can sit, quiet in the mornings but for the birds chirping and you touch my lips and every time is like the first time. I love how we can sit, to catch up together with old friends, how you still affect me from the inside out as if I could ever ignore you. I am jealous when I see you with others instead of me; don't you know how much I adore you, love you, need you? Don't you realize what you've done to me? You've intertwined yourself so deep in my everyday that to be without you would be blasphemy. There's no other way to explain it. Is this really as one-sided as you make it seem sometimes though? I'm always the one putting in the effort to make this work, to make you give me what I so desperately want and need from you. You must think I am crazy saying all of this but you must know it's you who's done this to me. It's you who I will never have enough of. It's you who I don't think I can live without..

article: Wings were the most common, at first. Everyone wanted wings mostly feathery, but a few black and leathery ones as well. That fad died out quickly enough once people realized that the human body didn't have a canvas big enough to allow for wings that could actually support it's weight. There's still plenty of dramatic aesthetic body mods, adding horns or turning skin blue or green, but the most common now are the little things. Eyebrows with a little more arch, smoother skin, getting rid of moles or freckles. Light lines and shadows suggesting muscle can encourage actual definition and growth. Then there are the specialty shops, the ones that change your race or gender. My grandmother tells me of a time when transgender folks were persecuted, when they had to live their lives in the wrong skin or take hormones. Now it's as simple as a large tattoo in the right place, encouraging the body to conform to what the mind knows and what the tattoo gun directs. The government has regulated what can be done, but they can only regulate what they know about. Invisible ink or UV light tattoos can still do the job. Tat hackers find ways to push the human body to it's limits, little waves of lines and codes that edge the human that much closer to the superhuman. The internet whispers of people with hollow bones that can take flight, people who can read your mind, people who can start fires with a flick of their wrist. Every once in a while someone comes forward with a supposed new ability, but it rarely is as impressive as they claim. That's because we know it's best to operate in the shadows. Our abilities do us no good if our every move is scrutinized by the media. I am, supposedly, the first of my kind, but I'm sure there will be more. A few specific squiggles of ink at the base of my skull and the world came into sharper focus around me; thoughts and emotions as apparent as the spoken word in the air around people. I'm still working on how to read the signs, but I'm getting there. I have a line from an organization very interested in someone of my skills working for them; I think they might be government, but I'm not sure. For now, I haven't paid for my own meal in three days, so I'm doing alright. I'm content enough to start small. I'll be moving up soon enough.

Arctic floorboard creaked and groaned with the sudden strain of supporting a human, a man. In the blink of an eye, I had reached the ceramic and porcelain hall, a temple of white and light. The sounds of rushing water filled the room as the scalding water tore the weariness and sleep from my body and mind. I performed the morning ritual with the fervor of a Tibetan monk, my devotion complete and unwavering. The shower, the epitome of human ingenuity and engineering.
